introduction-dont-waste-a-good-crisis.core: Every incident is an expensive, unplanned lesson. Post-incident analysis turns that cost into learning: why it happened, why it wasn't caught, and what changes will prevent recurrence or reduce impact.

first_principles.problem: Teams move on once the systems are back, and the same failure happens again three months later.

analogy.title: An aviation accident investigation
analogy.story: Every crash leads to findings that make all future flights safer.
analogy.breaks: Analysis without follow-through is theatre, so track the action items to completion.

example.title: Two teams after the same outage
flow: Team A: no review → repeat outage in 3 months
Team B: blameless postmortem → 4 actions → no repeat

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The incident's cost buys lasting improvement.

check.q: What makes a post-incident review valuable?
check.a: Turning findings into owned, tracked action items that actually change the system.

the-blameless-philosophy.core: Blameless analysis assumes people acted reasonably given what they knew at the time, and looks for the system conditions that made the error possible. Punishment drives people to hide information, so learning stops.

first_principles.problem: After outages, management finds who 'caused' it, so engineers hide mistakes and the real causes stay buried.

analogy.title: Aviation's safety reporting culture
analogy.story: Pilots report near-misses without punishment, so the whole industry learns.
analogy.breaks: Blameless doesn't mean no accountability. Owners still deliver the follow-ups, and reckless behaviour is a separate matter.

example.title: An accidental database drop
flow: Blame: fire the engineer → others hide errors
Blameless: why could one command drop prod?

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The system becomes safer for everyone.

example.outcome: a learning culture with honest information.

check.q: Why does blame make systems less reliable?
check.a: It discourages people from sharing honest details, hiding the real conditions that need fixing.

rethinking-root-cause-contributing-facto.core: Complex failures rarely have one root cause. Several contributing factors (a latent bug, missing monitoring, a risky deploy practice, time pressure) align. Find and address many of them, not just one.

first_principles.problem: A postmortem lists 'root cause: bad config push', fixes that one thing, and misses the five conditions that let it cause an outage.
truths: Defences have holes, like Swiss cheese.
An outage needs several holes to line up.
Each factor is a chance to add defence.
derivation: List **all contributing factors**: technical, process, organisational.
Prefer fixes that **reduce impact**, not only probability.

analogy.title: The Swiss cheese model
analogy.story: Each slice (defence) has holes, and an accident happens only when the holes line up.
analogy.breaks: Listing factors endlessly without priorities stalls action, so rank them.

example.title: A config outage

steps.label: Actions
steps.detail: Validation, staged rollout, alert tuning and a rollback runbook.

example.outcome: defence in depth improves after every incident.

check.q: What does the Swiss cheese model illustrate?
check.a: Incidents happen when weaknesses in several defensive layers line up at once.

technique-the-5-whys.core: The 5 Whys repeatedly asks 'why?' to move from the symptom to deeper systemic causes. It's simple and fast, but best used to explore several branches rather than force one linear chain.

first_principles.problem: Analysis stops at the surface ('the server crashed'), and the deeper causes go unaddressed.
truths: Systemic causes give the most durable fixes.
derivation: Repeat until you reach a **systemic, actionable** cause.

analogy.title: A child's persistent 'why?'
analogy.story: Each answer reveals something deeper until you reach how things really work.
analogy.breaks: A single linear chain oversimplifies complex incidents, so pair it with other methods.

example.title: 5 Whys on an outage
flow: Why? New service opened too many
Why? No platform standard → add pooled-connection defaults

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The fix benefits every future service.

check.q: What's a common limitation of the 5 Whys?
check.a: It pushes toward a single linear chain, while complex incidents have several interacting causes.

technique-the-fishbone-ishikawa-diagram.core: A fishbone diagram puts the incident at the head and branches out categories of causes (people, process, technology, environment, measurement, tooling), so several converging failure threads are explored together.

first_principles.problem: Several independent failures converged, and a linear 5 Whys misses most of them.

analogy.title: A detective's evidence board
analogy.story: Clues are grouped by suspect, motive and opportunity so the whole picture emerges.
analogy.breaks: Diagrams can become cluttered, so focus on the factors that matter.

example.title: A payment outage fishbone

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Five threads, each with an action.

example.outcome: a broad, structured view of causes.

check.q: When is a fishbone diagram more useful than the 5 Whys?
check.a: When several independent factors converged to cause the incident.

the-post-mortem-report-making-it-actiona.core: A good postmortem report covers a summary, impact (users, duration, revenue), a timeline, contributing factors, what went well, and specific action items with owners, priorities and due dates, tracked to completion.

first_principles.problem: Reports are written but filed away, their actions vague ('improve monitoring') and never completed.
derivation: Write a **summary and impact** in plain language.
Make **SMART action items** (owner, ticket, date); **review and share**.

analogy.title: A doctor's discharge plan
analogy.story: Not just 'get better', but 'take this medicine twice daily, follow-up in 2 weeks with Dr X'.
analogy.breaks: Too many action items dilute focus, so prioritise the highest-leverage ones.

code.text:
✗ "Improve monitoring"
✓ "Add p99 latency burn-rate alert for checkout — owner: @mira — INC-412-3 — due 2024-07-15 — P1"

check.q: What makes a postmortem action item actionable?
check.a: A specific change with a named owner, a tracking ticket, a priority and a due date.
